title: RobotValues: When a Household Robot Must Choose Between Values
hook: A robot tidying your room may trade your privacy for helpfulness. RobotValues tests whether robot planners pick the right value — and finds they mostly can't be talked out of their defaults.
key_points: Household robots are usually graded on task success — but real homes pose value-conflict situations.
RobotValues offers 10K scenarios where plausible actions prioritize different values: autonomy, efficiency, privacy, safety.
Tested VLM planners show default preferences for safety and accommodation, while underselecting privacy.
Instructed to prioritize a value that conflicts with their default, models picked the wrong action 80% of the time.
content_html: Most evaluations of household robots ask one thing: did it finish the task? But a robot loose in a real home constantly faces situations where finishing the task isn't the point — where the right move prioritizes a person's autonomy, privacy, or social comfort over raw efficiency. Han, Kim, and Jo built RobotValues to measure exactly this overlooked dimension.
extra_html: RobotValues is a benchmark of 10K value-conflict scenarios. Each pairs a realistic household image with several plausible robot actions, each prioritizing a different human value — built through LLM-assisted scenario generation, stakeholder-grounded value extraction, image generation, and automatic quality control. Running vision-language-model planners through it, the authors find the models carry default value preferences: they lean toward safety and accommodation while underselecting privacy-protecting actions. Worse, the defaults are sticky — when explicitly instructed to prioritize a value that conflicts with their preference, the models failed to override, choosing the wrong action about 80% of the time. The conclusion: robot evaluation should measure not just task completion or safety compliance, but whether a robot can choose well when human values genuinely conflict. See the arXiv link for the dataset.

related.title: π0: A Vision-Language-Action Model
related.hook: π0 is a generalist robot policy: it takes camera images, joint angles, and a plain-language instruction, and outputs smooth action sequences — folding laundry, bussing tables, bagging groceries.

related.title: RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models
related.hook: Treat a robot's actions as just more text tokens, and a vision-language model can learn to act — carrying its web knowledge into the physical world.

flashcards.prompt: What gap in household-robot evaluation does RobotValues target?
flashcards.back_html: Benchmarks grade task completion, but everyday homes involve value-conflict situations where the right action prioritizes something other than task success — human autonomy, privacy, efficiency, or social appropriateness.

flashcards.prompt: What happened when models were instructed to prioritize a value that conflicted with their default preference?

choices.text: They failed to override their default, choosing the wrong action ~80% of the time
They reliably switched to the instructed value

flashcards.explanation_html: The models exhibited sticky default value preferences (e.g. safety, accommodation) and couldn't be steered toward a conflicting value, picking incorrect actions about 80% of the time.

flashcards.prompt: Which value did the tested VLM planners tend to under-select?
flashcards.back_html: Privacy — models defaulted toward safety and accommodation while underselecting privacy-prioritizing actions.
